Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I have permanently changed for the worse
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Thanh, a 35-year-old South Eastern Asian male accountant, has experienced severe trauma after being subjected to torture. His life has been irrevocably altered by this event, and he is now seeking help due to the overwhelming distress it continues to cause him. Threatening memories of his torture often come unbidden into Thanh's mind, making everyday interactions extraordinarily challenging. Just recently, during a routine meeting at work with unfamiliar colleagues, the memory of being restrained and interrogated suddenly flooded back. The trigger was not just the presence of strangers but also their attempts to discuss future plans for the company’s financial health. This sudden intrusion of memories left Thanh feeling acutely vulnerable and fearful. Thanh has come to believe that he can never truly know who might harm him, a fear that intensifies with each intrusive memory. The trauma has permanently changed his perspective on trust and safety. He is convinced that he would have been able to prevent the torture if only someone else had stepped in, which compounds his feelings of helplessness and self-blame. These negative appraisals profoundly influence how Thanh processes and re-experiences his memories. For instance, when he recalls the torture, it feels as though these events belong to someone else—a disconnected film playing over and over again, with no clear order or sequence. This sense of detachment from his own memory makes it difficult for him to integrate the traumatic event into a coherent narrative. Thanh’s intrusive thoughts about the future are particularly distressing because they reinforce his belief that harm could happen again at any moment. He finds it nearly impossible to plan ahead without feeling an overwhelming sense of dread and anxiety. This constant fear has led Thanh to avoid social interactions and professional gatherings, further isolating him from the support he needs. His negative beliefs about himself and others have also impacted his relationships. Since his divorce, Thanh has struggled to form new connections, as each encounter with a stranger triggers intense memories of his torture. He is certain that only by maintaining distance can he protect himself from potential harm, but this avoidance has left him feeling profoundly alone. The intensity of these symptoms and the realization that they are significantly impacting his daily life have finally pushed Thanh to seek help. What frightens him most is not just the intrusive memories themselves but the fear that he will never feel safe again. He hopes for a way to regain control over his thoughts, find peace with his past, and perhaps rekindle hope in a safer future. Thanh's journey towards healing has begun, driven by an urgent need to break free from the relentless cycle of trauma and mistrust.
